etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English blade, blad, from Old English blæd (“leaf”), from Proto-West Germanic *blad, from Proto-Germanic *bladą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰl̥h₃-o-to-m, from *bʰleh₃- (“to thrive, bloom”).

See also West Frisian bled, Dutch blad, German Blatt, Danish blad, Irish bláth (“flower”), Welsh blodyn (“flower”), Tocharian A pält, Tocharian B pilta (“leaf”), Albanian fletë (“leaf”). Similar usage in German Sägeblatt (“saw blade”, literally “saw leaf”). Doublet of blat. More at blow.

definitions.definition: (metonymically) A sword or knife.

quote.citation: 1984, 2:08:29 from the start, in Dune‎[1] (Science Fiction), →OCLC:
quote.text: Paul: Give the Harkonnen a blade and let him stand forth.Shaddam IV: If Feyd wishes, he can meet you with my blade in his hand.

definitions.definition: Short for razor blade.
The (typically sharp-edged) part of a knife, sword, razor, or other tool with which it cuts.

quote.citation: 1904, Great Britain. War Office, Dress Regulations for the Officers of the Army (including the Militia): 1904, page 100:
quote.text: Sword. — The blade is straight, tapers gradually, is 32 9/16 inches long from shoulder to point, and is fullered on both sides, commencing 2 inches from the shoulder, to about 17 inches from the point, to a thickness of ·035 inch.

definitions.definition: The flat functional end or piece of a propeller, oar, hockey stick, chisel, screwdriver, skate, etc.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Lee S. Langston, “The Adaptable Gas Turbine”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Turbines have been around for a long time—windmills and water wheels are early examples. The name comes from the Latin turbo, meaning vortex, and thus the defining property of a turbine is that a fluid or gas turns the blades of a rotor, which is attached to a shaft that can perform useful work.

definitions.definition: The narrow leaf of a grass or cereal.
(botany) The thin, flat part of a plant leaf, attached to a stem (petiole).
A flat bone, especially the shoulder blade.
A cut of beef from near the shoulder blade (part of the chuck).
(chiefly phonetics, phonology) The part of the tongue just behind the tip, used to make laminal consonants.
(archaeology) A piece of prepared, sharp-edged stone, often flint, at least twice as long as it is wide; a long flake of ground-edge stone or knapped vitreous stone.
(ultimate frisbee) A throw characterized by a tight parabolic trajectory due to a steep lateral attitude.
(sailing) The rudder, daggerboard, or centerboard of a vessel.
A bulldozer or surface-grading machine with mechanically adjustable blade that is nominally perpendicular to the forward motion of the vehicle.
(dated) A dashing young man.

quote.citation: 1834 [1799], Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Robert Southey, “The Devil's Thoughts”, in The Poetical Works of S. T. Coleridge, volume II, London: W. Pickering, page 85:
quote.text: He saw a Turnkey in a trice / Unfetter a troublesome blade;

quote.citation: 1832, The Universal Songster: Or, Museum of Mirth, page 189:
quote.text: But very often blust'ring blades / Are Jerry Sneaks at home.

quote.citation: 1948, Jack Lait, Lee Mortimer, New York: Confidential!, Crown, published 1951, page 94:
quote.text: Vice does not thrive here, because the young blades seek it elsewhere.

quote.citation: 2009, Amanda Vickery, Behind Closed Doors, Yale University Press, page 77:
quote.text: Young blades were expected to kick over the traces and skirt disaster, before they graduated to matrimonial housekeeping.

definitions.definition: (slang, chiefly US) A homosexual, usually male.
(slang, chiefly US) An area of a city which is commonly known for prostitution.
Thin plate, foil.
(photography) One of a series of small plates that make up the aperture or the shutter of a camera.
(architecture, in the plural) The principal rafters of a roof.[1]
(biology) The four large shell plates on the sides, and the five large ones of the middle, of the carapace of the sea turtle, which yield the best tortoise shell.[2]
(computing) Short for blade server.
(climbing) Synonym of knifeblade

(mathematics) An exterior product of vectors. (The product may have more than two factors. Also, a scalar counts as a 0-blade, a vector as a 1-blade; an exterior product of k vectors may be called a k-blade.)
The part of a key that is inserted into the lock.
(athletics, informal) An artificial foot used by amputee athletes, shaped like an upside-down question mark.
(uncountable, music) The quality of singing with a pure, resonant sound; especially of a countertenor.
(informal) To skate on rollerblades.
(transitive) To furnish with a blade.
(intransitive, poetic) To put forth or have a blade.

quote.citation: 1633, Phineas Fletcher, “Elisa”, in Piscatorie Eclogues and other Poetical Miscellanies:
quote.text: As sweet a plant, as fair a flower, is faded / As ever in the Muses' garden bladed.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To stab with a blade
(transitive, professional wrestling, slang) To cut (a person) so as to provoke bleeding.
